# Onboard Guide: Behavioral Health and Psychological Support

## Applies When
- Self-reported mood score drops to ≤5 (on 1–10 scale) or perceived stress score rises to ≥6.
- Crew member expresses signs of interpersonal friction, cognitive fatigue, withdrawal from crew meals, or acute homesickness.
- Mission duration reaches high-stress milestones (e.g. mission midpoint, extended isolation, or anomaly recovery phases).

## Action Steps
1. Engage in structured daily off-duty time: spend at least 45 minutes on self-selected non-operational activities (reading, music, personal audio journal, or viewing Earth through the cupola/window).
2. Schedule a private psychological conference (PPC) or video communication with designated family and personal ground support contacts.
3. Conduct 15–20 minutes of daily mindfulness, progressive muscle relaxation, or guided breathing exercises in quiet crew quarters.
4. Maintain a regular circadian schedule: align personal meal, work, exercise, and sleep times consistently with Greenwich Mean Time (GMT) mission timeline.
5. Participate in communal crew bonding activities, such as shared evening meals, cooperative game time, or movie viewing.
6. Discuss workload pacing and task prioritization with the mission commander to redistribute high-stress work packets if needed.
7. Record mood and stress levels honestly in the daily confidential check-in log.

## Escalation Criteria
- Mood score drops to ≤3 or perceived stress score reaches ≥8.
- Persistent severe depressive symptoms, panic attacks, thoughts of self-harm, or active interpersonal conflict impairing mission safety.
- Marked cognitive impairment or refusal to carry out critical flight safety tasks.
- Contact ground flight surgeon and Crew Behavioral Health & Performance (BHP) officer immediately.

https://www.nasa.gov/hrp/research/behavioral-health
